claims.text: Premelting and melting in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by differential surface segregation driven by thermally activated atomic diffusion.
Copper has a lower melting point and higher atomic mobility than the other constituents of the Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles.
Heating causes copper to migrate preferentially to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-segregated copper forms a premelted, liquid-like layer.
The premelted copper-rich surface layer softens the particle and triggers subsequent bulk melting.
The selected starting nanoparticles are initially solid, single-phase, and nearly homogeneous in Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
Controlled heating from ambient temperature through premelting to complete melting provides the intervention needed to test the proposed mechanism.
Surface effects are significant for Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles in the tens-of-nanometers size range.
The structural mediator is a copper-enriched surface layer produced by differences in atomic mobility and surface energy.
Thermal energy activates diffusion among the constituent elements.
Copper's relatively weak bonding contributes to its segregation to the surface during heating.
The localized premelted surface layer reduces the effective melting temperature of the particle.
Surface-layer formation initiates a stepwise rather than homogeneous melting process.
Before complete melting, imaging and compositional mapping will detect gradual development of a copper-enriched, liquid-like surface layer.
The premelted layer will form at a lower temperature than in monometallic or bimetallic nanoparticles lacking pronounced segregation.
The proposed baseline systems do not exhibit comparable differential surface diffusion or marked elemental segregation during premelting.

The mechanism applies to equiatomic or near-equiatomic high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles in the tens-of-nanometers size regime when surface effects dominate and oxidation or other competing effects are absent.
Absence of preferential surface enrichment before bulk melting, or observation of homogeneous melting without a premelted surface layer, would falsify the hypothesis.
